{{short description|On the existence of arithmetic progressions in subsets of the natural numbers}}
{{for|Roth's theorem on Diophantine approximation of algebraic numbers|Roth's theorem}}
'''Roth's theorem on arithmetic progressions''' is a result in [[additive combinatorics]] concerning the existence of [[arithmetic progression]]s in subsets of the [[natural number]]s. It was first [[mathematical proof|proven]] by [[Klaus Roth]] in 1953.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Roth |first1=Klaus |title=On certain sets of integers |journal=Journal of the London Mathematical Society |date=1953 |volume=28 |issue=1 |pages=104–109 |doi=10.1112/jlms/s1-28.1.104}}</ref> Roth's theorem is a special case of [[Szemerédi's theorem]] for the case <math>k = 3</math>.

==Statement==
A subset ''A'' of the natural numbers is said to have positive upper density if

:<math>\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{|A\cap \{1, 2, 3, \dotsc, n\}|}{n} > 0</math>.

<blockquote>'''Roth's theorem on arithmetic progressions (infinite version)''': A subset of the natural numbers with positive upper density contains a {{nowrap|3-term}} arithmetic progression.</blockquote>

An alternate, more qualitative, formulation of the theorem is concerned with the maximum size of a [[Salem–Spencer set]] which is a subset of <math>[N] = \{1, \dots, N\}</math>. Let <math>r_3([N])</math> be the size of the largest subset of <math>[N]</math> which contains no {{nowrap|3-term}} arithmetic progression.

<blockquote>'''Roth's theorem on arithmetic progressions (finitary version)''': <math>r_3([N]) = o(N).</math></blockquote>

Improving [[upper and lower bounds]] on <math>r_3([N])</math> is still an open research problem.

==History==
The first result in this direction was [[Van der Waerden's theorem]] in 1927, which states that for sufficiently large N, coloring the integers <math>1, \dots, n</math> with <math>r</math> colors will result in a <math>k</math> term arithmetic progression.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=van der Waerden |first1=B. L. |author-link=Bartel Leendert van der Waerden |title=Beweis einer Baudetschen Vermutung |journal=Nieuw. Arch. Wisk. |date=1927 |volume=15 |pages=212–216}}</ref>

Later on in 1936 Erdős and Turán [[conjecture]]d a much stronger result that any subset of the integers with positive density contains arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions. In 1942, [[Raphaël Salem]] and [[Donald C. Spencer]] provided a construction of a 3-AP-free set (i.e. a set with no {{nowrap|3-term}} arithmetic progressions) of size <math>\frac{N}{e^{O(\log N/\log \log N)}}</math>,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Salem |first1=Raphaël |last2=Spencer |first2=Donald C. |title=On sets of integers which contain no three terms in arithmetical progression |journal=[[Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America]] |date=1942 |volume=28 |issue=12 |pages=561–563 |doi=10.1073/pnas.28.12.561 | doi-access=free |pmid=16588588 |pmc=1078539 |mr=0007405 |bibcode=1942PNAS...28..561S }}</ref> disproving an additional conjecture of Erdős and Turán that <math>r_3([N]) = N^{1 - \delta}</math> for some <math>\delta > 0</math>.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Erdös |first1=Paul |last2=Turán |first2=Paul |title=On Some Sequences of Integers |journal=Journal of the London Mathematical Society |date=1936 |volume=4 |issue=4 |pages=261–264 |mr=1574918 |doi=10.1112/jlms/s1-11.4.261 }}</ref>

In 1953, Roth partially resolved the initial conjecture by proving they must contain an arithmetic progression of length 3 using Fourier analytic methods. Eventually, in 1975, Szemerédi proved [[Szemerédi's theorem]] using combinatorial techniques, resolving the original conjecture in full.

==Proof techniques==
The original proof given by Roth used Fourier analytic methods. Later on another proof was given using [[Szemerédi's regularity lemma]].

===Proof sketch via Fourier analysis===

In 1953, Roth used [[Fourier analysis]] to prove an upper bound of <math>r_3([N]) = O\left(\frac{N}{\log \log N}\right)</math>. Below is a sketch of this proof.

Define the [[Fourier transform]] of a function <math>f : \mathbb{Z} \rightarrow \mathbb{C}</math> to be the function <math>\widehat{f} : [0, 1) \rightarrow \mathbb{C}</math> satisfying
:<math>\widehat{f}(\theta) = \sum_{x \in \mathbb{Z}}f(x)e(-x\theta)</math>,
where <math>e(t) = e^{2\pi i t}</math>.

Let <math>A</math> be a 3-AP-free subset of <math>\{1, \dots, N\}</math>. The proof proceeds in 3 steps.
# Show that a <math>A</math> admits a large Fourier coefficient.
# Deduce that there exists a sub-progression of <math>\{1, \dots, N\}</math> such that <math>A</math> has a density increment when restricted to this subprogression.
# Iterate Step 2 to obtain an upper bound on <math>|A|</math>.

====Step 1====

For functions, <math>f, g, h : \mathbb{Z} \rightarrow \mathbb{C},</math> define 
:<math>\Lambda(f, g, h) = \sum_{x, y \in \mathbb{Z}} f(x)g(x + y)h(x + 2y)</math>

<blockquote>'''Counting Lemma''' Let <math>f, g : \mathbb{Z} \rightarrow \mathbb{C}</math> satisfy <math>\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}|f(n)|^2, \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}|g(n)|^2 \le M</math>. Define <math>\Lambda_3(f) = \Lambda(f,f,f)</math>. Then <math>|\Lambda_3(f) - \Lambda_3(g)| \le 3M\|\widehat{f - g}\|_\infty</math>.
</blockquote>

The counting lemma tells us that if the Fourier Transforms of <math>f</math> and <math>g</math> are "close", then the number of {{nowrap|3-term}} arithmetic progressions between the two should also be "close." Let <math>\alpha = |A|/N</math> be the density of <math>A</math>. Define the functions <math>f = \mathbf{1}_{A}</math> (i.e the [[indicator function]] of <math>A</math>), and <math>g = \alpha \cdot \mathbf{1}_{[N]}</math>. Step 1 can then be deduced by applying the Counting Lemma to <math>f</math> and <math>g</math>, which tells us that there exists some <math>\theta</math> such that 
:<math>\left|\sum_{n=1}^N (1_A - \alpha)(n)e(\theta n) \right| \ge \frac{\alpha^2}{10}N</math>.

====Step 2====

Given the <math>\theta</math> from step 1, we first show that it's possible to split up <math>[N]</math> into relatively large subprogressions such that the character <math>x \mapsto e(x\theta)</math> is roughly constant on each subprogression.

<blockquote>'''Lemma 1:''' Let <math>0 < \eta < 1, \theta \in \mathbb{R}</math>. Assume that <math>N > C\eta^{-6}</math> for a universal constant <math>C</math>. Then it is possible to partition <math>[N]</math> into arithmetic progressions <math>P_i</math> with length <math>N^{1/3} \le |P_i| \le 2N^{1/3}</math> such that <math>\sup_{x, y \in P_i}|e(x\theta) - e(y\theta)| < \eta</math> for all <math>i</math>. </blockquote>

Next, we apply Lemma 1 to obtain a partition into subprogressions. We then use the fact that <math>\theta</math> produced a large coefficient in step 1 to show that one of these subprogressions must have a density increment:

<blockquote>'''Lemma 2:''' Let <math>A</math> be a 3-AP-free subset of <math>[N]</math>, with <math>|A| = \alpha N</math> and <math>N > C\alpha^{-12}</math>. Then, there exists a sub progression <math>P \subset [N]</math> such that <math>|P| \ge N^{1/3}</math> and <math>|A \cap P| \ge (\alpha + \alpha^2/40)|P|</math>.</blockquote>

====Step 3====
We now iterate step 2. Let <math>a_t</math> be the density of <math>A</math> after the <math>t</math>th iteration. We have that <math>\alpha_0 = \alpha,</math> and <math>\alpha_{t + 1} \ge \alpha + \alpha^2/40.</math> First, see that <math>\alpha</math> doubles (i.e. reach <math>T</math> such that <math>\alpha_T \ge 2\alpha_0</math>) after at most <math>40/\alpha + 1</math> steps. We double <math>\alpha</math> again (i.e reach <math>\alpha_T \ge 4\alpha_0</math>) after at most <math>20/\alpha + 1</math> steps. Since <math>\alpha \le 1</math>, this process must terminate after at most <math>O(1/\alpha)</math> steps.

Let <math>N_t</math> be the size of our current progression after <math>t</math> iterations. By Lemma 2, we can always continue the process whenever <math>N_t \ge C\alpha_t^{-12},</math> and thus when the process terminates we have that <math>N_t \le C\alpha_t^{-12} \le C\alpha^{-12}.</math> Also, note that when we pass to a subprogression, the size of our set decreases by a [[cube root]]. Therefore
:<math>N \le N_t^{3^t} \le (C\alpha^{-12})^{3^{O(1/\alpha)}} = e^{e^{O(1/\alpha)}}.</math>
Therefore <math>\alpha = O(1/\log \log N),</math> so <math>|A| = O \left(\frac{N}{\log \log N}\right),</math> as desired. <math>\blacksquare</math>

Unfortunately, this technique does not generalize directly to larger arithmetic progressions to prove Szemerédi's theorem. An extension of this proof eluded mathematicians for decades until 1998, when [[Timothy Gowers]] developed the field of higher-order Fourier analysis specifically to generalize the above proof to prove Szemerédi's theorem.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Gowers |first1=W. T.|title=A new proof of Szemerédi's theorem for arithmetic progressions of length four |journal=[[Geometric and Functional Analysis]] |date=1998 |volume=8 |issue=3 |pages=529–551 |doi=10.1007/s000390050065 | doi-access=free}}</ref>

=== Proof sketch via graph regularity ===
From the [[Szemerédi regularity lemma]] and [[counting lemma]] one obtains the [[graph removal lemma]], and as a corollary the following:

'''Diamond-free Lemma.''' Any graph <math>G</math> on <math>n</math> vertices in which every edge lies in precisely one unique triangle has <math>o(n^2)</math> edges.

==== Application to Roth’s theorem ====
First note that a set <math>A\subseteq\{1,\dots,N\}</math> has a 3-term arithmetic progression iff its reduction modulo <math>M:=2N+1</math> does.

Fix <math>A\subseteq \{1,\dots,N\}</math> with no 3-term AP. Construct a tripartite graph <math>G</math> with parts <math>X,Y,Z</math>, each a copy of <math>\mathbb{Z}/M\mathbb{Z}</math>. Add edges as follows:
* <math>x\in X</math> to <math>y\in Y</math> if <math>y-x\in A</math>;
* <math>y\in Y</math> to <math>z\in Z</math> if <math>z-y\in A</math>;
* <math>z\in Z</math> to <math>x\in X</math> if <math>(x-z)/2\in A</math> (since 2 is invertible mod <math>M</math>).

If <math>x,y,z</math> form a triangle, then
<math>y-x,\ \frac{x-z}{2},\ z-y\in A</math>. These three numbers form an arithmetic progression in that order with step <math>(x+z-2y)/2</math>. Because <math>A</math> has no nontrivial 3-term AP, they are equal, so  <math>(x+z-2y)/2=0</math>. Therefore, if we fix any two vertices of <math>G</math> connected by an edge, every triangle extending this edge must satisfy <math>x+z-2y=0</math>, yielding a unique choice of the third vertex. Furthermore, such a choice guarantees the existence of the other two edges in that triangle. Thus, the diamond-free lemma applies, and <math>e(G)=o((3M)^2)=o(N^2)</math>.

Notice now, that each element <math>a \in A</math> contributes exactly one edge for each vertex in a part: for instance, for every <math>x \in X</math>, there is exactly one <math>y \in Y</math> such that <math>y - x \equiv a \pmod{M}</math>, so <math>a</math> gives exactly <math>M</math> edges between <math>X</math> and <math>Y</math>. The same holds for the other two pairs, hence <math>e(G)=3|A|M</math>. Consequently,

<math>
|A| = \frac{e(G)}{3M} = \frac{o(N^2)}{3(2N+1)} = o(N)
</math>

proving Roth’s theorem.

==Extensions and generalizations==
Szemerédi's theorem resolved the original conjecture and generalized Roth's theorem to arithmetic progressions of arbitrary length. Since then it has been extended in multiple fashions to create new and interesting results.

[[Hillel Furstenberg|Furstenberg]] and [[Yitzhak Katznelson|Katznelson]]<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Furstenberg | first1=Hillel | author1link=Hillel Furstenberg | last2=Katznelson | first2=Yitzhak | author2link=Yitzhak Katznelson | title=An ergodic Szemerédi theorem for commuting transformations | journal=[[Journal d'Analyse Mathématique]] | doi=10.1007/BF02790016 | doi-access=free | mr=531279 | volume=38 | year=1978 | pages=275–291 | issue=1| s2cid=123386017 }}</ref> used [[ergodic theory]] to prove a multidimensional version and Leibman and [[Vitaly Bergelson|Bergelson]]<ref>{{cite journal | first1=Vitaly | last1=Bergelson | author1link=Vitaly Bergelson | first2=Alexander | last2=Leibman | title=Polynomial extensions of van der Waerden's and Szemerédi's theorems | journal=[[Journal of the American Mathematical Society]] | volume=9 | issue=3 | year=1996 | pages=725–753 | mr=1325795 | doi=10.1090/S0894-0347-96-00194-4| doi-access=free }}</ref> extended it to polynomial progressions as well. Most recently, [[Ben J. Green|Green]] and [[Terence Tao|Tao]] proved the [[Green–Tao theorem]] which says that the [[prime number]]s contain arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions. Since the prime numbers are a subset of density 0, they introduced a "relative" Szemerédi theorem which applies to subsets with density 0 that satisfy certain [[pseudorandomness]] conditions. Later on [[David Conlon|Conlon]], [[Jacob Fox|Fox]], and Zhao<ref>{{cite journal | first1=David | last1=Conlon | author1link=David Conlon | first2=Jacob | last2=Fox | author2link=Jacob Fox | first3=Yufei | last3=Zhao | title=A relative Szemerédi theorem | arxiv=1305.5440 | year=2015 | mr=3361771 | volume=25 | issue=3 | pages=733–762 | doi=10.1007/s00039-015-0324-9 | doi-access=free | journal=[[Geometric and Functional Analysis]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | first=Yufei | last=Zhao | title=An arithmetic transference proof of a relative Szemerédi theorem | journal=[[Mathematical Proceedings of the Cambridge Philosophical Society]] | volume=156 | year=2014 | pages=255–261 | issue=2 | mr=3177868 | doi=10.1017/S0305004113000662| arxiv=1307.4959 | bibcode=2014MPCPS.156..255Z | s2cid=119673319 }}</ref> strengthened this theorem by weakening the necessary pseudorandomness condition. In 2020, Bloom and Sisask<ref name=":0">Thomas F. Bloom, Olof Sisask, ''Breaking the logarithmic barrier in Roth's theorem on arithmetic progressions'', [[arxiv:2007.03528|arXiv:2007.03528]], 2020</ref>  proved that any set <math>A</math> such that <math>\sum_{n \in A} \frac{1}{n}</math> diverges must contain arithmetic progressions of length 3; this is the first non-trivial case of another [[Erdős conjecture on arithmetic progressions|conjecture]] of [[Paul Erdős|Erdős]] postulating that any such set must in fact contain arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions.

===Improving bounds===
{{See also|Szemerédi's_theorem#Quantitative bounds|Erdős conjecture on arithmetic progressions#Progress and related results|Salem–Spencer set#Size}}

There has also been work done on improving the bound in Roth's theorem. The bound from the original proof of Roth's theorem showed that

:<math>r_3([N]) \leq c\cdot\frac{N}{\log\log N}</math>

for some constant <math>c</math>. Over the years this bound has been continually lowered by Szemerédi,<ref>{{cite journal|first=Endre|last=Szemerédi|title=Integer sets containing no arithmetic progressions|journal=[[Acta Mathematica Hungarica]]|year=1990|volume=56|issue=1–2|doi=10.1007/BF01903717|doi-access=free|mr=1100788|pages=155–158}}</ref> [[Roger Heath-Brown|Heath-Brown]],<ref>{{cite journal|author-link=D. R. Heath-Brown|first=Roger|last=Heath-Brown|title=Integer sets containing no arithmetic progressions|volume=35|journal=[[Journal of the London Mathematical Society]]|issue=3|year=1987|mr=889362|pages=385–394|doi=10.1112/jlms/s2-35.3.385}}</ref> [[Jean Bourgain|Bourgain]],<ref>{{cite journal|author-link=Jean Bourgain|first=Jean|last=Bourgain|title=On triples in arithmetic progression|journal=[[Geometric and Functional Analysis]]|volume=9|issue=5|year=1999|pages=968–984|mr=1726234|doi=10.1007/s000390050105|s2cid=392820 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|author-link=Jean Bourgain|first=Jean|last=Bourgain|title=Roth's theorem on progressions revisited|volume=104|year=2008|pages=155–192|journal=[[Journal d'Analyse Mathématique]]|mr=2403433|doi=10.1007/s11854-008-0020-x|doi-access=free|issue=1|s2cid=16985451 }}</ref> and [[Tom Sanders (mathematician)|Sanders]].<ref>{{cite journal|author-link=Tom Sanders (mathematician)|first=Tom|last=Sanders|title=On certain other sets of integers|journal=[[Annals of Mathematics]]|volume=185|issue=1|year=2012|pages=53–82|mr=2892617|doi=10.1007/s11854-012-0003-9|arxiv=1007.5444|s2cid=119727492 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|author-link=Tom Sanders (mathematician)|first=Tom|last=Sanders|title=On Roth's theorem on progressions|journal=[[Annals of Mathematics]]|volume=174|issue=1|year=2011|pages=619–636|mr=2811612|doi=10.4007/annals.2011.174.1.20|arxiv=1011.0104|s2cid=53331882 }}</ref> The current (July 2020) best bound is due to Bloom and Sisask<ref name=":0" /> who have shown the existence of an absolute constant c>0 such that

:<math>r_3([N]) \leq \frac{N}{(\log N)^{1+c}}.</math>

In February 2023 a preprint<ref>{{Cite arXiv |eprint=2302.05537 |class=math.NT |first1=Zander |last1=Kelley |first2=Raghu |last2=Meka |title=Strong Bounds for 3-Progressions |date=2023-02-10}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Sloman |first=Leila |date=2023-03-21 |title=Surprise Computer Science Proof Stuns Mathematicians |url=https://www.quantamagazine.org/surprise-computer-science-proof-stuns-mathematicians-20230321/ |access-date= |website=Quanta Magazine |language=en}}</ref> (later published<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Kelley |first1=Zander |last2=Meka |first2=Raghu |chapter=Strong Bounds for 3-Progressions |date=2023-11-06 |title=2023 IEEE 64th Annual Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science (FOCS) |publisher=IEEE |pages=933–973 |doi=10.1109/FOCS57990.2023.00059 |isbn=979-8-3503-1894-4|arxiv=2302.05537 }}</ref>) by Kelley and Meka gave a new bound of:

<math>r_3([N]) \leq 2^{-\Omega((\log N)^{1/12})} \cdot N</math>.

Four days later, Bloom and Sisask published a preprint giving an exposition of the result<ref>{{Cite journal |arxiv=2302.07211 |first1=Thomas F. |last1=Bloom |first2=Olof |last2=Sisask |title=The Kelley–Meka bounds for sets free of three-term arithmetic progressions |journal=Essential Number Theory |date=2023-02-14|volume=2 |pages=15–44 |doi=10.2140/ent.2023.2.15 }}</ref> (later published<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Bloom |first1=Thomas F. |last2=Sisask |first2=Olof |date=2023-12-31 |title=The Kelley–Meka bounds for sets free of three-term arithmetic progressions |url=https://msp.org/ent/2023/2-1/p02.xhtml |journal=Essential Number Theory |language=en |volume=2 |issue=1 |pages=15–44 |doi=10.2140/ent.2023.2.15 |issn=2834-4634|arxiv=2302.07211 }}</ref>), simplifying the argument and yielding some additional applications. Several months later, Bloom and Sisask obtained a further improvement to <math>r_3([N]) \leq \exp(-c(\log N)^{1/9})N</math>, and stated (without proof) that their techniques can be used to show <math>r_3([N]) \leq \exp(-c(\log N)^{5/41})N</math>.<ref>{{Cite arXiv |last1=Bloom |first1=Thomas F. |last2=Sisask |first2=Olof |date=2023-09-05 |title=An improvement to the Kelley-Meka bounds on three-term arithmetic progressions |class=math.NT |eprint=2309.02353 }}</ref>

In a 2026 preprint,<ref>{{cite arXiv |last=Raghavan |first=Rushil |title=Improved Bounds for 3-Progressions |date=2026-05-15 |class=math.NT |eprint=2603.27045 }}</ref> Raghavan reported further improved bounds, proving:

<math>|A| \leq \exp(-c\log(N)^{1/6}\log\log(N)^{-1/6})N</math>.

There has also been work done on the other end, constructing the largest set with no {{nowrap|3-term}} arithmetic progressions. The best construction has barely been improved since 1946 when [[Felix Behrend|Behrend]]<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Behrend |first1=F. A. |title=On sets of integers which contain no three terms in arithmetical progression |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America |date=1946 |volume=32 |issue=12 |pages=331–332 |doi=10.1073/pnas.32.12.331 | doi-access=free|pmid=16578230 |pmc=1078964 |bibcode=1946PNAS...32..331B }}</ref> improved on the initial construction by Salem and Spencer and proved

:<math>r_3([N]) \geq N\exp(-c\sqrt{\log N})</math>.

Due to no improvements in over 70 years, it is conjectured that Behrend's set is asymptotically very close in size to the largest possible set with no {{nowrap|3-term}} progressions.<ref name=":0" /> If correct, the Kelley-Meka bound will prove this conjecture.

===Roth's theorem in finite fields===
As a variation, we can consider the analogous problem over [[finite field]]s. Consider the finite field <math>\mathbb{F}_3^n</math>, and let <math>r_3(\mathbb{F}_3^n)</math> be the size of the largest subset of <math>\mathbb{F}_3^n</math> which contains no {{nowrap|3-term}} arithmetic progression. This problem is actually equivalent to the [[cap set]] problem, which asks for the largest subset of <math>\mathbb{F}_3^n</math> such that no 3 points lie on a line. The cap set problem can be seen as a generalization of the card game [[Set (card game)|Set]].

In 1982, Brown and Buhler<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Brown |first1=T. C. |authorlink1=Tom Brown (mathematician) |last2=Buhler |first2=J. P. |title=A density version of a geometric Ramsey theorem |journal=[[Journal of Combinatorial Theory]] | series=Series A |date=1982 |volume=32 |issue=1 |pages=20–34|doi=10.1016/0097-3165(82)90062-0 |doi-access=free }}</ref> were the first to show that <math>r_3(\mathbb{F}_3^n) = o(3^n).</math> In 1995, Roy Mesuhlam<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Mesuhlam |first1=Roy |title=On subsets of finite abelian groups with no 3-term arithmetic progressions |journal=[[Journal of Combinatorial Theory]] | series=Series A |volume=71 |issue=1 |pages=168–172 |doi=10.1016/0097-3165(95)90024-1|year=1995 |doi-access=free }}</ref> used a similar technique to the Fourier-analytic proof of Roth's theorem to show that <math>r_3(\mathbb{F}_3^n) = O\left(\frac{3^n}{n}\right).</math> This bound was improved to <math>O(3^n/n^{1 + \epsilon})</math> in 2012 by Bateman and Katz.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bateman |first1=M. |last2=Katz |first2=N. |title=New bounds on cap sets |journal=Journal of the American Mathematical Society |date=2012 |volume=25 |issue=2 |pages=585–613|doi=10.1090/S0894-0347-2011-00725-X |doi-access=free |hdl=2022/19057 |hdl-access=free |arxiv=1101.5851 }}</ref>

In 2016, [[Ernie Croot]], Vsevolod Lev, Péter Pál Pach, [[Jordan Ellenberg]] and Dion Gijswijt developed a new technique based on the polynomial method to prove that <math>r_3(\mathbb{F}_3^n) = O(2.756^n)</math>.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Ellenberg |first1=Jordan S. |last2=Gijswijt |first2=Dion |title=On large subsets of <math>\mathbb{F}_q^n</math> with no three-term arithmetic progression |journal=Annals of Mathematics, Second Series |volume=185 |issue=1 |pages=339–343 |doi=10.4007/annals.2017.185.1.8 |arxiv=1605.09223 |year=2016 |s2cid=119683140 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Croot |first1=Ernie |last2=Lev |first2=Vsevolod F. |last3=Pach |first3=Péter Pál |title=Progression-free sets in <math>\mathbb{Z}_{4}^{n}</math> are exponentially small |arxiv=1605.01506 | journal= [[Annals of Mathematics]] | series=2nd series | pages=331–337 | volume=185 | date=2017 | issue=1 | doi=10.4007/annals.2017.185.1.7}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Klarreich |first1=Erica |title=Simple Set Game Proof Stuns Mathematicians |url=https://www.quantamagazine.org/20160531-set-proof-stuns-mathematicians/ |website=Quanta |date=May 31, 2016}}</ref>

The best known lower bound is <math>2.2202^{n}</math>, discovered in December 2023 by [[Google DeepMind]] researchers using a [[large language model]] (LLM).<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Romera-Paredes |first1=Bernardino |last2=Barekatain |first2=Mohammadamin |last3=Novikov |first3=Alexander |last4=Balog |first4=Matej |last5=Kumar |first5=M. Pawan |last6=Dupont |first6=Emilien |last7=Ruiz |first7=Francisco J. R. |last8=Ellenberg |first8=Jordan S. |last9=Wang |first9=Pengming |last10=Fawzi |first10=Omar |last11=Kohli |first11=Pushmeet |last12=Fawzi |first12=Alhussein |date=2023-12-14 |title=Mathematical discoveries from program search with large language models |journal=Nature |volume=625 |issue=7995 |language=en |pages=468–475 |doi=10.1038/s41586-023-06924-6 |issn=1476-4687|doi-access=free |pmid=38096900 |pmc=10794145 }}</ref>

===Roth's theorem with popular differences===

Another generalization of Roth's theorem shows that for positive density subsets, there not only exists a {{nowrap|3-term}} arithmetic progression, but that there exist many 3-APs all with the same common difference.

<blockquote>'''Roth's theorem with popular differences:''' For all <math>\epsilon > 0</math>, there exists some <math>n_0 = n_0(\epsilon)</math> such that for every <math>n > n_0</math> and <math>A \subset \mathbb{F}_3^n</math> with <math>|A| = \alpha3^n,</math> there exists some <math>y \neq 0</math> such that <math>|\{x : x, x + y, x + 2y \in A\}| \ge (\alpha^3 - \epsilon)3^n.</math></blockquote>

If <math>A</math> is chosen randomly from <math>\mathbb{F}_3^n,</math> then we would expect there to be <math>\alpha^33^n</math> progressions for each value of <math>y</math>. The popular differences theorem thus states that for each <math>|A|</math> with positive density, there is some <math>y</math> such that the number of 3-APs with common difference <math>y</math> is close to what we would expect.

This theorem was first proven by Green in 2005,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Green |first1=Ben |title=A Szemerédi-type regularity lemma in abelian groups, with applications |journal=[[Geometric and Functional Analysis]] |date=2005 |volume=15 |issue=2 |pages=340–376 |mr=2153903 |doi=10.1007/s00039-005-0509-8 |doi-access=free}}</ref> who gave a bound of <math>n_0 = \text{tow}((1/\epsilon)^{O(1)}),</math> where <math>\text{tow}</math> is the tower function. In 2019, Fox and Pham recently improved the bound to <math>n_0 = \text{tow}(O(\log\frac{1}{\epsilon})).</math><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Fox |first1=Jacob | authorlink1=Jacob Fox |last2=Pham |first2=Huy Tuan |title=Popular progression differences in vector spaces | journal=International Mathematics Research Notices | volume=2021 | issue=7 | date=April 2021 | pages=5261–5289 | doi=10.1093/imrn/rny240 | doi-access=free |arxiv=1708.08482 |bibcode=2017arXiv170808482F}}</ref>

A corresponding statement is also true in <math>\mathbb{Z}</math> for both 3-APs and 4-APs.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Green |first1=Ben |title=An Irregular Mind |last2=Tao |first2=Terrence  |date=2010 |volume=21 |pages=261–334 |publisher=Bolyai Society Mathematical Studies|doi=10.1007/978-3-642-14444-8_7 |bibcode=2010arXiv1002.2028G |arxiv=1002.2028 |series=Bolyai Society Mathematical Studies |isbn=978-3-642-14443-1 |chapter=An Arithmetic Regularity Lemma, an Associated Counting Lemma, and Applications |s2cid=115174575 }}</ref> However, the claim has been shown to be false for 5-APs.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bergelson |first1=Vitaly |last2=Host |first2=Bernard |last3=Kra |first3=Bryna |title=Multiple recurrence and nilsequences. With an appendix by Imre Ruzsa |journal=Inventiones Mathematicae |date=2005 |volume=160 |issue=2 |pages=261–303|doi=10.1007/s00222-004-0428-6 |s2cid=1380361 }}</ref>
